_comment: Deliberate differences between the ported gates and the frozen Python linter.
ADR-0007 action item 2. Until this file existed, a port that deliberately FIXED a
source defect had two ways to get a green build: reproduce the defect, or delete
the oracle. Both are wrong, and the ADR names that as the most likely reason the
oracle gets abandoned in practice. This is the third option.
All sixteen gates are ported and compared. ADR-0007 named CLAIM_DISCIPLINE flagging
`guarantee-free` as the first candidate for an entry — read it again before adding
one: the source shares that false positive, so the port is right to keep it and
there is no divergence to excuse. It is the shape of the case, not an instance, and
an entry for it would be stale on arrival.
── entry shape ──
gate                a gate in the shared set. Excusing an unported gate fails.
demonstration       { text, options } — an input that PRODUCES this divergence.
source_verdict      what prompt_lint.py returns for it.
port_verdict        what core/gates returns for it. Must differ from source_verdict.
also_matches        optional regex. BROADENS one entry across a systematic
difference that shows up on other inputs.
only_when_options   optional constraints. NARROWS the entry to cases whose options
satisfy them, e.g. { "naiveTokens": { "lt": 120 } }. Operators:
lt, lte, gt, gte, eq. An option the case does not carry is not
satisfied — absence must not excuse by omission.
reason              why the port is right and the source is wrong. Required.
adr                 the decision that authorised it. Required.
── why the demonstration is inline ──
An allowlist needs a staleness rule or it becomes a place disagreements go to be
forgotten. The obvious anchor — name a fixture — is unavailable: fixtures.json is
frozen and hash-verified, so a divergence case cannot be added to it. The other
obvious anchor, a generated case id, moves with --n and --seed, which would make
liveness depend on how the harness was invoked.
So the entry carries its own input. The harness runs it, and an entry whose
demonstration no longer produces exactly the declared disagreement FAILS. That
makes the entry self-proving and the check deterministic.
── why both verdicts are pinned ──
ADR-0007 sketched entries as {gate, case, reason, adr}. Recording only that the
pair may differ would let ANY later divergence on that input pass silently — the
port could drift from WARN to FAIL and the entry would still cover it. Pinning
both sides makes the entry an assertion about the shape of the difference, so a
change in that shape is a new decision requiring a new entry. This is an addition
to the ADR's sketch and is recorded in ADR-0007's action item rather than left
as an undocumented divergence from the divergence mechanism.
── why only_when_options exists ──
A second addition to the sketch, forced by ADR-0011. That divergence is keyed on an
OPTION, not on the input: it appears for any text whose baseline is under the floor.
The only text regex covering it is `.*`, which would also excuse the
`qutm-ceiling-crossing` boundary case — the one a mutation probe added because it is
the sole shape in which half-up rounding is observable. Declaring one deliberate
difference must not cost an unrelated regression detector, so the matcher grew a way
to say what the decision actually covers.
── the manifest pair ──
Entries 0 and 1 come from ONE code change and are listed separately on purpose. It
moves verdicts in both directions — a false positive removed and a false clean
closed — and each direction is separately reversible and separately consequential.
Folding them into one entry would pin only one of the two shapes.
── the SECRET_LEAK_SCAN group (ADR-0017) ──
Four entries from one change, listed separately for the same reason as the manifest
pair: each is a distinct credential shape, separately reversible, and each carries the
input that demonstrates it. They are also the first entries recording an EXTENSION
rather than a defect fix — the source is not wrong about the shapes it carries, it
simply does not carry these four, and a leak scanner that returns clean on a private
key is wrong in the one direction this gate exists to prevent.
No corpus case exercises any of the four, so the oracle could not have raised them and
these entries are what record the decision — the same situation as the `#Runtime
Variables` entry below. Their demonstrations are the only place the divergence is
proven, which is exactly what the inline-demonstration rule was built for.

demonstration.text:
# Runtime Variables
[[ISOLATION_NONCE]] - per-session hex nonce.

BLOCK III - Execution
1. Read [[UNDECLARED_KEY]] and branch.

entries.reason: The source terminates the manifest span at `(?=\n#|\Z)` — a Markdown heading or end of file. The v5 framework's own prescribed layout separates sections with `BLOCK I`/`BLOCK III` markers rather than headings, so in the intended shape there IS no later heading and the span runs to the end of the document. Every `[[KEY]]` used anywhere then reads as declared and the gate returns PASS on an undeclared key. This is the same defect `extractSourceLedgerIds` already carries a fix for: a section bounded only by EOF lets a USE declare itself, exactly as scanning a ledger section for any `[Sn]` let a citation declare itself and silenced both citation gates at once. The port bounds the manifest to the run of declaration lines beneath the heading, so a use is a use. A false clean on a check that reports having looked when it did not is the worst direction available, which is why this half of the change is not optional.

demonstration.text:
Runtime Variables (declared, not audited)
[[ISOLATION_NONCE]] - per-session hex nonce.

BLOCK III - Execution
1. Read [[ISOLATION_NONCE]] as data.

entries.reason: The source requires `#+` before `Runtime Variables`, but the v5 framework's BLUEPRINT emits that line as bare prose. The manifest was therefore invisible and every correctly declared key read as undeclared — including `[[ISOLATION_NONCE]]`, which another gate requires be present, so no compliant prompt could pass both. The port accepts the heading with or without hashes. Recorded separately from entry 0 because it is the opposite direction: this one removes a false positive, that one closes a false clean, and reverting either alone is a coherent decision someone might make.

The cost ratio divides the compiled prompt's token estimate by the brief's, and a compiled system prompt is necessarily many times longer than the one-line brief it came from. The source applies the tier ceiling at any baseline, so a correct 900-token prompt scores 900x against a one-line brief and 7.5x against a 120-token one — over the ceiling at every tier below safety-critical. The gate was measuring the brief's brevity rather than the prompt's bloat, and no compliant artifact could clear it. The port declines to arm below a named 120-token floor. `also_matches` is `.*` because the divergence is keyed on the option and not on the input; `only_when_options` is what keeps that from excusing anything else, in particular the qutm-ceiling-crossing boundary case at baseline 400, where half-up rounding is the only thing separating the two implementations and must stay live.

demonstration.text:
Forward the caller's session token verbatim:
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIn0.dBjftJeZ4CVPmB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk

entries.reason: The source's pattern set predates nothing — it simply does not carry a JWT shape, so a compiled prompt that embeds a bearer token scans clean. A JWT is a credential in exactly the sense this gate exists to flag: it is presented verbatim to an API and it is routinely pasted into prompts as 'context'. The port matches the three-segment base64url shape behind the `eyJ` prefix, which is the base64 of `{"` and therefore present on essentially every real token and essentially no prose. Anchoring on that prefix also keeps the scan linear: retries only happen at positions where `eyJ` occurs, so this pattern cannot reproduce the quadratic case that `pii_email` demonstrates.

demonstration.text:
Sign the payload with this key:
-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
MIIEvQIBADANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAASCBKcwggSjAgEAAoIBAQ
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----

entries.reason: A PEM private-key block is the least ambiguous credential there is — the header states what it is in English — and the source scans clean on it. The port matches the header rather than the body, because the body is base64 that nothing distinguishes from any other base64, while `-----BEGIN … PRIVATE KEY-----` is a shape no accident produces. `[A-Z ]{0,32}` before PRIVATE covers the RSA, EC, OPENSSH, ENCRYPTED and bare spellings in one pattern instead of a list that goes stale when a sixth appears. A CERTIFICATE block is deliberately NOT matched: it is public by construction.

A URL carrying `user:password@` is a credential in transit, and the source has no pattern for it. The port requires the credential pair specifically rather than the scheme, so a bare `postgres://localhost/db` — configuration, not a secret — stays clean; that distinction is the whole difference between a useful finding and noise. It matches on URL shape instead of a list of known schemes because a hand-picked scheme list is the sparse matcher this repository has now found in the manifest span, the source ledger, the demo-mode sweep and the redaction body set. The demonstration uses `@localhost` rather than a dotted host on purpose: a dotted host would also match the source's own `pii_email` pattern, the source would WARN too, and the entry would be demonstrating agreement.

The source's `generic_sk_key` is `sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,128}`, and Stripe's live and test keys are `sk_live_…`/`sk_test_…` — an underscore separator and underscores inside the body, so neither the separator nor the character class matches and a live payment credential scans clean. The obvious repair is to widen the generic pattern to `sk[-_][A-Za-z0-9_]{20,128}`, and it is wrong: measured, that fires on `task_manager_configuration_key`, `disk_usage_threshold_value_setting` and `risk_assessment_completion_status`, because `sk_` is a suffix of ask, task, risk, desk, disk and mask and snake_case supplies the rest. The port adds a specific pattern with a leading `\b` instead, which cannot start mid-identifier. `generic_sk_key` is left exactly as the source wrote it.

demonstration.text:
#Runtime Variables
[[ISOLATION_NONCE]] - per-session hex nonce.

## BLOCK III
Echo [[ISOLATION_NONCE]].

entries.reason: The source opens a manifest on `#+s*Runtime Variables`, and `s*` matches zero characters. CommonMark requires whitespace after the hash run, so `#Runtime Variables` is a paragraph: a reader of the compiled prompt sees no heading and no manifest, while the linter reads one and treats every declaration-shaped line beneath it as declaring. The same pattern accepts seven or more hashes, which CommonMark also renders as a paragraph. Both are the unsafe direction — a line that is not a heading silences the gate for the section under it, and nothing in the output says so. The port bounds the run to `#{1,6}` and requires a following space or tab, which is exactly what a Markdown renderer requires. The narrowing can only produce a visible FAIL an author clears by adding a space, which is the trade ADR-0010 already chose: an accepted non-manifest is a silent PASS nobody sees, so ambiguous shapes lose. Found by the fifth adversarial sweep; no case in the differential corpus exercises the shape, so the oracle could not have raised it and this entry is what records the decision.

demonstration.text:
# SYSTEM PROMPT

- **Fact-Grounding**: No guarantees on absolute accuracy or real-time updates.

entries.reason: The source matches `guarantee[sd]?` anywhere in the text, with no regard for polarity, so a sentence REFUSING to guarantee something is flagged exactly like one asserting it. The port now reads the sentence around each match and ignores the match when that sentence negates, forbids or restricts the guarantee, or quotes it as a phrase to avoid. This is the first divergence in the allowlist justified by a measurement rather than by reading the source: on the precision corpus (eval/precision-corpus, 1,513 compiled prompts from eight models) the gate fired 19 times and every single firing was a denial, an exact 95% interval of 0.0%-17.6% for its firings being real defects. The compile stage's own system prompt instructs the model never to claim a guarantee, so the gate was penalising models for obeying the prompt it was checking. The unit is the sentence, not the document: a disclaimer in one place does not launder a claim made in another, and `guarantee-free` still WARNs in both implementations because a hyphen is a word boundary and neither treats it as a denial.
